newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa says farm sector hampers EU trade talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa says farm sector hampers EU trade talks.

text.p: The exclusion of much of South Africa's agricultural production from a proposed free trade agreement with the European Union continues to hamper talks, foreign trade relations chief director Faizel Ismail said on Wednesday.

"Until we have a clear indication that some real progress is going to be made in reducing the rather long list of exclusions from the trade agreement, South Africa will find it very difficult to proceed with the trade part of the negotiations with any enthusiasm," he said.
The EU has granted South Africa limited accession to the Lome Convention, but has said that a separate free trade agreement should be negotiated.
South Africa claims that the proposed free trade agreement will exclude 39 percent of its farm exports.
The exclusion was despite the fact that some of the agricultural products were not produced in Europe, or would only be exported when they were out of season in Europe.

Ismail was briefing a joint sitting of the parliamentary trade and industry, agriculture and foreign affairs committees after the latest round of negotiations between South Africa and the EU in Johannesburg this week.
The next EU-South African ministerial review of the negotiations is scheduled for July.

Another sticking point was the reluctance of the EU to recognise that South Africa would have to implement significant tariff adjustments as part of the agreement, in addition to its present World Trade Organisation commitments, he said.
"We feel that significant efforts have to be made by the EU to provide a package of measures which will address this," Ismail said.
He envisaged a special fund to provide investment in new industries and re-training of workers to counter lost jobs and capacity.

"We are still waiting for a response by the EU," he said, Ismail said that the negotaitions would also have to take into consideration the possible trade diversionary effects on South African's neighbouring states.
Concern had already been expressed about the fact that subsidised and duty-free beef imports from the EU could affect producers in Botswana and Namibia.
